stem: During an emergency red-cell transfusion before the recipient's ABO type is known, why may group O red blood cells be selected?

options.A: Group O red blood cells lack A and B antigens and can be used for recipients of other ABO groups when emergency red-cell transfusion is required before typing is known.
options.B: Group O red blood cells are universal recipients and can receive red cells from every ABO group.
options.C: Group O red blood cells express both A and B antigens, which makes them compatible with all recipients.
options.D: AB plasma and group O red cells use the same ABO compatibility rule because plasma and red-cell compatibility are interchangeable.

rationale: AABB states that in an emergency anyone can receive type O red blood cells, which is why people with type O blood are commonly described as universal red-cell donors. This ABO red-cell compatibility principle is different from plasma compatibility; AABB separately notes that individuals of all ABO types can receive AB plasma. Therefore A is correct. B reverses donor/recipient terminology, C incorrectly states that group O red cells express A and B antigens, and D incorrectly treats red-cell and plasma compatibility as interchangeable. Rh selection and other compatibility considerations are outside the deliberately limited ABO-red-cell scope of this item.
educational_objective: Recognize group O red cells as the ABO-compatible emergency red-cell choice when recipient ABO type is not yet known, while distinguishing red-cell compatibility from plasma compatibility and avoiding overgeneralization to Rh selection.
source_organization: Association for the Advancement of Blood & Biotherapies (AABB)
source_document_title: FAQs About Blood and Blood Donation
source_locator: About Blood > Most common blood type: in an emergency, anyone can receive type O red blood cells; people with type O blood are known as universal donors. The same section states that individuals of all types can receive type AB plasma, demonstrating component-specific ABO compatibility.
source_claim_supported: For ABO red-cell compatibility, group O red cells can be used in emergencies before a recipient's ABO type is known; this does not mean group O is a universal recipient or that plasma compatibility follows the same rule.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current AABB transfusion/donor guidance; NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.exact_locator: AABB FAQ About Blood > emergency type O red cells and AB plasma statement
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item is intentionally restricted to ABO red-cell compatibility before typing and explicitly does not claim universal Rh compatibility or interchangeability with plasma rules.

distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because group O describes universal RBC donor status, not universal recipient status.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because group O RBCs lack A and B antigens rather than expressing both.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because ABO compatibility rules differ by blood component; AB plasma compatibility is not the same rule as O RBC compatibility.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A correctly explains emergency ABO red-cell selection without reversing donor/recipient or plasma rules.
audit_findings.cueing: All options concern ABO transfusion compatibility and component rules.
audit_findings.blueprint: Reduction of Risk Potential — transfusion compatibility and adverse-event prevention.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked current AABB FAQ, emergency O RBC statement, AB plasma distinction, all alternatives, rationale, objective, scope limitations, ambiguity, cueing and NCSBN mapping. A remained uniquely correct.
